Agreed to run a 72-hour benchmark using customer traffic and to share configs and spreadsheets.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-09
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Bianca (Redwood SRE), Daniel (Nimbus CTO), Maya (Platform Eng), Oliver (Security)

Auto-generated summary (may be noisy): Discussed autoscale burst policy, queueing behavior when concurrency saturates, reserved capacity sizing, and security constraints for VPC/private deployment, next steps include benchmarks and sharing config.

[00:00] Aisha: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick intro from our side, marco is our se, bianca is on the s r e team who owns the benchmarks and cost models
[00:12] Daniel: hi thanks, excited to dive in, we basically want to understand how redwood would behave during a weekly spike and what guarantees we can get for p95 and p99
[00:22] Marco: cool, so at a high level we operate with a hybrid policy - reserved pools for steady state and burst-on-demand for spikes, we can do autoscale rules based on qps or token rate, and there are queueing knobs if you want to bound concurrency
[00:36] Maya: can you clarify "burst-on-demand" does that mean we'll pay a big premium for the burst or is it a soft overage?
[00:44] Bianca: good question, pricing depends on contract - during pilot you'll likely see usage-based billing for burst. Technically the runtime routes to on-demand nodes in another pool, there's a slight cold-start risk but we mitigate with warm standby slots and pre-warming heuristics
[00:58] Oliver: from security we also need to know if burst nodes can be inside our vpc or if they cross into shared infra
[01:06] Marco: for private deployments yes we can keep everything in your VPC, for hosted dedicated we isolate data but the burst pool may be regionally routed; we have a private-only flavour for full isolation but that requires reserved capacity
[01:18] Daniel: what about queueing, like when concurrent long-decoding requests saturate gpus will requests get queued and what's the timeout behavior?
[01:28] Marco: we use a hybrid queue with priority buckets, by default user requests join a fast-path queue for under-100ms decode jobs, long jobs get a separate lane; you can configure max queue time and reject thresholds. Typical default is 10s max queue before we return 503 but you can change to 30s if you're okay with latency tail
[01:45] Aisha: note that queueing trades latency for higher effective throughput, so we generally tune to your p95 SLOs
[01:51] Maya: do you have a recommended queueing model for health-care bursts? we can't drop requests but we can accept slightly higher latency up to 5s p95
[02:00] Bianca: i'd recommend a two-tier policy: reserved baseline to meet 99% of normal traffic, burst pool for spikes, and tight queueing with 5s max for non-critical paths. Also enable prefix KV cache for repeated prompts to cut decode time
[02:15] Daniel: KV cache sizing - how do we estimate RAM/GPU KV cache need for our n=200k active patients?
[02:23] Marco: KV cache is primarily per-session and depends on avg prompt length and session reuse. For 200k active users if only 5% are concurrent and average context growth is 1k tokens, you can approximate KV RAM by sessions * avg_kv_per_session * bytes_per_token. We usually run a short profiler to get concrete numbers, marco: we should run that with their sample traffic
[02:40] (small cross talk)
[02:45] Maya: some of these numbers are fuzzy, can you do that profiling for us?
[02:48] Marco: yes that's in action items, we'll run a workload-based run and give recommended cache sizing
[02:53] Oliver: quantization - will 4-bit quant reduce latency? is there major output quality impact for our clinical text generation?
[03:00] Bianca: quantization reduces memory footprint which can reduce batching pressure and sometimes improves throughput, but it can add a small jitters in output. For clinical text we recommend running an eval on a private subset; per our experience int8 or Q4f16 tends to be safe for many instruction models but check for hallucination increase
[03:20] Daniel: so tradeoff is cost and throughput vs strict output fidelity, understood
[03:24] Aisha: another knob is batching; larger batches improve token/sec throughput but increase per-request latency. we often recommend dynamic batching where small requests go through low-latency path and heavy batching happens when tokens pending exceed threshold
[03:38] Marco: and the runtime supports continuous-batching optimizations to avoid token fragmentation, we can show graphs from the benchmarks
[03:45] Maya: for pilot we'd like p95 under 2s for short prompts (<=128 tokens) and p99 under 5s, are those reasonable with a reserved baseline?
[03:53] Bianca: yes, with a right-sized dedicated pool and caching for hot prompts that's doable; the sizing depends on average concurrency and the percent of long-running decodes. We'll need your qps distribution to produce numbers
[04:05] Daniel: here's a quick rundown of our traffic: baseline 60 rps, nightly spikes to 450 rps for 10 minutes, weekly big spike 2k rps for 2 minutes. We need to handle 2k bursts without SLA failure ideally
[04:20] Marco: for those microbursts we recommend a burst policy with pre-warmed standby nodes and a short term overcommit. Config: reserved capacity to handle 80% of baseline, standby for 100-200 qps and on-demand auto-scale for sudden jumps. Also set a request reject policy for non-critical endpoints to protect core workflows
[04:40] Aisha: quick note on cost: fully reserved GPUs priced lower per-token. Burst on-demand usually has a higher per-token cost. Usually customers accept a small burst premium because otherwise they'd overprovision for rare spikes
[04:53] Oliver: are there circuit breakers if a bad prompt causes runaway token generation? we need to ensure we don't overload budget or hardware
[04:59] Marco: yes we have token/length caps and real-time cost limits per-key. Also per-route limits and automatic model fallback to cheaper smaller variants when thresholds hit
[05:10] Maya: curious about model fallback, does that change the API response shape?
[05:14] Marco: no, response shape is same. You can configure degradations: e.g., fallback to lower-spec model with slightly higher perplexity but similar prompt/template support. You can also set A/B style rollout to measure quality delta
[05:26] Daniel: let's talk more concrete, can you show a queueing model example with numbers?
[05:30] Marco: sure, consider an 8-gpu pool where each gpu has throughput of 400 tokens/sec for your model at baseline. If avg request is 512 tokens that's around 0.32 requests/sec per GPU. For 60 rps baseline we need X GPUs - keep in mind decoding steps vary. We usually convert to token/sec then add headroom for p99 and burst margin
[05:51] Bianca: i'll annotate the spreadsheet with example calculations. we'll include p50,p95,p99 assumptions and the headroom multiplier (1.2-1.5) we recommend
[06:00] (discussion moves to warm starts and pre-warming heuristics)
[06:10] Marco: warm standby is effectively pre-allocating a subset of nodes that are kept hot with small inference pings. It's a balance - live standby costs more but reduces cold-start tail latency to sub-second
[06:24] Maya: how many standby nodes would you recommend for our 2k rps 2-minute spike?
[06:30] Marco: depends on your acceptable p99. For a 2-minute spike it's often cheaper to have 4-8 standby nodes and rely on fast on-demand scaling for the rest. We'll calculate precise numbers in the benchmark report
[06:42] Daniel: curious about the math for queueing — are you using M/M/c or some other queueing model?
[06:47] Marco: we model using M/G/c approximations because service times are heavy-tailed due to variable token lengths. We simulate using your traffic profile to get more accurate tail behavior rather than pure closed-form approximations
[06:59] Oliver: from security perspective, if we do private deployment will autoscaling call home or require any external endpoints? we need to avoid egress for some environments
[07:08] Bianca: private on-prem package can be fully air-gapped; for VPC it depends on whether you want control-plane connectivity to Redwood managed services. We can do a customer-managed control plane where telemetry is pushed to your endpoints only
[07:22] Aisha: important to note, some features like fully-managed burst may require Redwood control-plane involvement, we can scope that in SOW if needed
[07:30] Daniel: ok, good to know. can you explain reserved GPUs vs soft reservations?
[07:34] Marco: reserved GPUs are capacity you pay for or commit to, guaranteed to you. Soft reservations are like ephemeral reservations with faster spin-up but not guaranteed in extreme contention. For enterprise SLAs we recommend firm reserved pools for critical workloads
[07:47] Maya: what about autoscale cooldowns and step-scaling? our traffic has microbursts that could cause flapping if cooldowns are too long
[07:56] Marco: we support step-scaling with short cooldown windows and rate-limited scale-up to avoid flapping, we also have predictive scaling heuristics based on historical patterns to pre-scale for known scheduled spikes
[08:08] (brief silence then crosstalk)
[08:12] Aisha: bianca do we have a recommended default config we can share?
[08:15] Bianca: yes i'll attach a starter policy in the follow-up: reserved baseline, 8% standby, burst-on-demand with max 5x scale factor, queue time 5s for non-critical endpoints, drop policy for unimportant routes
[08:30] Daniel: what observability will we get to validate the pilot? token-level breakdowns? per-route p95?
[08:35] Bianca: console gives token-level cost and latency, per-model and per-route charts, trace ids and exportable logs. we'll also provide a perf spreadsheet with the benchmark outputs
[08:45] Maya: does the KV cache persist across restarts and how is it encrypted at rest?
[08:50] Marco: KV cache in GPU memory is ephemeral but we can persist checkpointed cache to customer-managed storage; encryption at rest uses your KMS if deployed in your VPC, and all network paths are TLS secured
[09:03] Oliver: SOC2 questions: do you provide audit logs for admin actions and who accessed what model?
[09:09] Bianca: yes audit logs, SSO/SAML, role-based access control, and exportable compliance reports. we'll share our security pack in the next step
[09:17] (participants short notes)
[09:20] Aisha: let's talk pilot success metrics briefly - what are you measuring?
[09:24] Daniel: p95 latency for short prompts, cost per 1k tokens baseline vs pilot, error rate, and no data egress breaches
[09:31] Maya: also cache hit rate and model quality delta after quantization if we test those profiles
[09:36] Bianca: perfect, we'll include those in the benchmark and evaluate tradeoffs
[09:40] (mid-call, detailed example calculations are shared verbally by Marco)
[09:44] Marco: example: if you want p95 < 2s for <=128 token requests, we size to token/sec then use 1.3 headroom. For your 60 rps baseline assuming avg 64 tokens per request that's 3840 tokens/sec baseline. If a gpu handles 2500 tokens/sec (with quantization benefits) you'd need 2 gpus baseline but for headroom and p99 you'd reserve 4. For burst to 2k rps for 2mins you'd rely on standby + on-demand to add 8-12 extra gpus quickly
[10:05] Daniel: that's helpful, but can we see that in a spreadsheet with your assumptions?
[10:09] Bianca: yes, we'll send the sheet, including different model profiles (full fp16, Q4, int8) and the per-token throughput numbers we measured
[10:16] Maya: is there a recommended approach to limit cost during bursts besides throttling requests? like preemptible instances?
[10:22] Marco: we support a mixed pool using lower-cost preemptible/spot GPUs for burst, with fallback to on-demand if spots are reclaimed. There's also rate-limiter per-key to avoid runaway spend
[10:34] Oliver: what SLA do you commit to on private deployments?
[10:38] Aisha: private SLA depends on contract but we have options for 99.9%+ with dedicated support, we can include runbook handoff and playbooks in the SOW
[10:48] (discussion about running a proof-of-concept)
[10:52] Marco: proposed pilot: 2-week run with traffic replay, 72-hour high-fidelity benchmark, include quantization comparisons and KV cache sizing. We'll run three configs: reserved-only, reserved+burst, reserved+burst+spots. We'll provide cost and latency tradeoffs for each
[11:06] Daniel: timeline sounds fine, we'll aim to provide sample traffic and keys by Friday
[11:11] Aisha: recap next steps: marcos runs benchmark, bianca shares spreadsheets and security pack, daniel provides traffic. schedule follow up week of 9/22 to review results
[11:20] (closing remarks and thanks)
[11:25] Daniel: thanks everyone, appreciate the level of detail
[11:27] Aisha: thanks all we'll follow up with docs and invite for next call
